source.title_on_document: Human-AI Collaboration for Brainstorming: Effect of the Presence of AI Ideas on Breadth of Exploration

supplement.holds: No supplement or appendix is referenced or included in this PDF. The earlier study described as under review is a separate study report, not an identified supplement (PDF pp. 1 and 4). Main-text results contain tests and a rank-biserial correlation, but no arm SDs, SEs, or confidence intervals for the main contrasts.

paper_design_summary: This paper reanalyzes a randomized experiment conducted in university informatics courses, with 52 students analyzed after two exclusions; students brainstormed individually about reducing food waste either alone or with on-demand GPT-3.5 idea suggestions (PDF pp. 1, 4–5). A student assistant blind to condition classified ideas into predefined categories, and the authors compared the number of categories covered per participant, both including accepted AI ideas and restricting to human-authored ideas, plus idea counts and within-category fluency (PDF pp. 5–6). Additional descriptive analyses compare category distributions and new-category contributions by human versus AI origin within the same dataset (PDF pp. 6–7).

studies.label: Food-waste brainstorming experiment: reanalysis of flexibility

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individual students were assigned to human-only brainstorming or human+AI brainstorming. The experiment was conducted in three courses at the authors' university's informatics department. Course-based setting is coded field_rct under the codebook; classes were not the assignment unit (PDF p. 4, section 3.1; p. 5, section 4).
assignment.quote: Participants were randomly assigned to conditions and were equally distributed across conditions (human-only: 26, human+ai: 26).
assignment.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 4, Results; setting and conditions: PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.1.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration is stated in the PDF.

arms.name: human+AI
arms.description: Individual brainstorming in the app with on-demand AI suggestions. Participants were asked to request suggestions at least once; suggestions appeared in a separate list and could be copied into the participant's own list. Only accepted suggestions counted toward the submitted result (PDF p. 4, sections 3.1–3.2). Analyzed arm count: PDF p. 5, section 4.

arms.name: human-only
arms.description: Individual brainstorming in the same study's baseline condition without generative-AI suggestions (PDF p. 4, section 3.1). Analyzed arm count: PDF p. 5, section 4.

participants.exclusions: The paper reports 54 participants and excludes two students' data for incomplete data and a misunderstanding of the task, leaving 52 analyzed. It does not explicitly give the number randomized before exclusions or the excluded students' assigned arms, so randomized counts are left null. Separately, seven uncategorized ideas and all deleted ideas were excluded from the idea corpus; the number of deleted ideas is not stated (PDF p. 5, sections 3.3 and 4).
participants.who: University students enrolled mostly in informatics study programs; recruited through the university's courses on design science research, computer-supported cooperative work, and data-driven solutions for the smart city. The document describes the university as Western European (PDF pp. 4–5, sections 3.1, 3.3 and 4).
participants.quote: The remaining 52 participants (age: mean=22.3, min=18, max=37 years old; gender: 8 female, 44 male) were university students enrolled mostly in informatics study programs.
participants.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), section 4, Results, for people, exclusions and arm counts; PDF p. 4, section 3.1, for courses; PDF p. 5, section 3.3, for region and idea exclusions.

ai_tool.how_used: A custom brainstorming app supplied three AI ideas per request in a separate panel; participants could copy suggestions into their own list or use them as stimuli. Prompts incorporated the brainstorming question, the participant's ideas, and previous AI ideas; temperature was 0.9. This was on-demand supply of complete ideas rather than free-form chatbot use (PDF p. 4, section 3.2 and Figure 2; p. 5, opening paragraph).

task.description: Generate ideas addressing 'How can we reduce food waste?' Participants brainstormed individually, then selected their best ideas and completed a post-questionnaire. The scored flexibility outcomes concern brainstorming idea lists, not a separate assessment after AI removal (PDF p. 4, section 3.1; pp. 5–6, section 4.1).
task.duration: 10 minutes of brainstorming; about 30 minutes for the whole study (PDF p. 4, section 3.1).

outcomes.name: Flexibility of the submitted idea list, including accepted AI ideas (H1)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Count of distinct categories covered by each participant's idea list, using the predefined Specht and Buck system with 13 categories in five clusters. An assistant blind to condition categorized the ideas. The human+AI lists include 115 accepted/copied AI suggestions, not all 373 logged AI suggestions (PDF p. 5, section 3.3 and beginning of section 4.1; p. 6, section 4.1). Despite the paper's 'team' label, each observation is the list of one human participant, with or without AI.

contrasts.reported: human+AI mdn=5; human-only mdn=2; Mann-Whitney U=546.5, p<.001; rank-biserial correlation rB=.617. The text also reports mean=4.115 for category coverage without identifying it as an arm-specific mean. No arm SDs, SEs or CIs are printed; rB is the reported rank-biserial effect, not a standardized mean difference.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1 and Figure 3; inclusion of accepted AI ideas begins on PDF p. 5.

outcomes.name: Flexibility of human-authored ideas, excluding AI-origin ideas (H2)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of distinct categories among each participant's human-authored ideas, excluding AI-origin ideas in the human+AI condition. The same category coding is used as for H1. Human-authored ideas in the treatment were generated while AI suggestions were available (PDF pp. 4–6). Figure 4 presents boxplots; unlabeled arm medians were not estimated from the graph.

contrasts.reported: Mann-Whitney U=326.0, p=.830; no significant between-condition difference. The text reports mean=2.846 for category coverage without identifying it as an arm-specific mean. An accompanying association between human idea number and categories covered is reported as Spearman's ρ=.817, p<.001; this is a correlation, not an AI-treatment effect.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1, paragraphs surrounding Figure 4.

outcomes.name: Human within-category fluency
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Average number of human-authored ideas per category covered, calculated for each participant; participants contributing no ideas were assigned zero. This measures depth within the participant's categories, not similarity across people (PDF p. 6, section 4.1).

contrasts.reported: human-only mdn=2; human+ai mdn=1; Mann-Whitney U=119.0, p<.001. No arm SDs, SEs, CIs or standardized effect are printed.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.1, paragraph immediately before section 4.2.

outcomes.name: Number of human-authored ideas
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Human-origin idea counts and participant means by randomized condition, excluding AI-origin ideas. Table 2 supplies means and total idea counts, and section 4 supplies analyzed arm sizes; SDs are absent. The statistics_available descriptor refers to the available arm descriptives only, not to a complete mean/SD/n package.

contrasts.reported: Table 2: human+AI human-origin ideas=87 (mean=3.3); human-only human-origin ideas=140 (mean=5.4); human-origin total=227. Section 4 reports 26 analyzed people per arm. Section 4.1 says human-only participants contributed significantly more ideas and refers to the earlier under-review study, but gives no quantity test statistic or p value. Section 5.1 instead says there was no significant difference in the number of human ideas. Direction reflects the printed means; the significance claim is internally inconsistent.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Table 2 and section 4; PDF p. 6, section 4.1; conflicting statement on PDF p. 8 (printed p. 428), section 5.1.

outcomes.name: Total logged idea quantity, including all retained AI suggestions
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Descriptive condition-level corpus counts from Table 2, combining human-origin ideas and all retained AI suggestions. These are not counts of final accepted idea lists: all retained AI suggestions enter this table, whereas the main flexibility analysis uses only accepted/copied suggestions. The table aggregates ideas within each condition; no combined participant mean or variance is given.

contrasts.reported: Table 2: human+AI total=460 ideas; human-only total=140 ideas; overall total=600 ideas. The human+AI corpus includes 373 AI-origin ideas (mean=14.3) and 87 human-origin ideas (mean=3.3). Section 5.1 states that humans with AI jointly produced significantly more ideas, but no corresponding test statistic or p value is printed. These are idea counts, not people or counts of accepted final outputs.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 5 (printed p. 425), Table 2; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), opening of section 5.1; accepted-suggestion distinction: PDF pp. 5–6, section 4.1.

outcomes.name: Pooled category coverage and distribution by human versus AI origin
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Descriptive category distribution and number of categories covered after pooling human-origin ideas across both randomized arms and AI-origin suggestions from the human+AI arm. Category-specific percentages are kept together as one distribution outcome. This is a comparison of interacting sources of ideas, not an independent model-versus-human experiment and not a measure of similarity across people's outputs. Figure 5 was checked directly in the PDF.

contrasts.control_arm: Human-origin ideas pooled across human+AI and human-only sessions
contrasts.reported: AI ideas cover all 13 categories; human ideas cover 12, with none in value-added products (section 4.2). Corpus sizes in Table 2: AI=373 ideas, human=227 ideas. Figure 5 percentages, human then AI: converting food waste into energy 1,3% / 0,8%; family and consumer science training 1,8% / 6,4%; food date labeling 2,2% / 1,6%; food waste for agricultural purposes 1,8% / 7,0%; food waste markets 7,0% / 8,0%; large-scale food donation 10,1% / 14,5%; legislating food waste reduction 12,3% / 9,9%; meal planning 7,9% / 1,1%; mobile technology 2,2% / 13,4%; public information campaigns 11,9% / 11,5%; smart technology 4,4% / 8,3%; value-added products AI 0,5% (no human bar; human absence is stated in the text); waste mitigation 37,0% / 16,9%. Decimal commas are retained from Figure 5. No inferential test or uncertainty interval is reported.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 6 (printed p. 426), section 4.2; PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), Figure 5 and accompanying paragraph; corpus counts: PDF p. 5, Table 2.

outcomes.name: Rate of introducing a new category after the brainstorming counterpart contributes
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Within human+AI sessions only, the authors chronologically ordered contributions and examined cases in which the human contributed after the AI or the AI contributed after the human. They report the fraction of contributions that explore new categories by source. The denominator of eligible contributions is not given. This is a process comparison within the assisted condition, not a randomized arm contrast.

contrasts.treatment_arm: AI contributions after human contributions, within human+AI sessions
contrasts.control_arm: Human contributions after AI contributions, within human+AI sessions
contrasts.reported: AI explores new categories in 41.2% of cases; humans explore new categories in 41.9% of cases. These are descriptive percentages; no denominator, test statistic, p value, SE or CI is reported. The discussion says both similarly drove exploration; no inferential equivalence is established.
contrasts.locator: PDF p. 7 (printed p. 427), section 4.2, final paragraph; interpretation continues across PDF pp. 7–8, section 5.1.

sample_overlap.shares_participants_with: An earlier human-AI brainstorming study, described only as under review, on idea quantity, novelty and value. Reuse of its data is explicit; this PDF does not identify the other paper by title, authors, DOI or candidate ID.
sample_overlap.quote: To answer this research question, we used data collected for a previous study (under review) focusing on human-AI brainstorming.
sample_overlap.locator: PDF p. 1 (printed p. 421), section 1, Introduction; also PDF p. 4 (printed p. 424), section 3.2, Data collection instrument.

company_involvement.description: No company authorship, funding or study partnership is stated. Both authors are affiliated with Universität Hamburg. Funding is attributed to the German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF), project HyMeKI. OpenAI supplied the model used as the intervention; tool use alone is not coded as company involvement.
company_involvement.locator: PDF p. 1, author affiliations; PDF p. 4, section 3.2, model; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 429), Acknowledgment.

eligibility.reason: Random assignment of individual students to AI assistance versus human-only brainstorming is explicit (PDF p. 5, section 4), and AI was available while the scored ideas were generated (PDF p. 4, sections 3.1–3.2). The same experiment has 52 analyzed people, 26 per arm, after two exclusions, meeting the 50-person rule (PDF p. 5, section 4). Idea categories were coded by an assistant blind to condition, and participant-level flexibility and fluency were scored on actual ideas (PDF p. 5, section 3.3; pp. 5–6, section 4.1). This is a reanalysis of an earlier experiment, requiring sample deduplication; it is not an independent new sample.

one_line_finding: With 52 students analyzed (PDF p. 5), accepted human+AI idea lists covered more categories than human-only lists (medians 5 vs 2; U=546.5, p<.001, rank-biserial rB=.617), but human-authored category coverage did not differ significantly (U=326.0, p=.830; PDF p. 6, section 4.1).
open_questions: Which publication is the earlier under-review study whose participants and data were reused? The PDF gives no bibliographic identity; resolve sample overlap before pooling.

What was the randomized count before exclusions, and which arms contained the two excluded students? The PDF gives 54 participants overall and 52 analyzed, but no explicit allocation counts at assignment (PDF p. 5, section 4).

Can the authors clarify the conflicting statements about human idea quantity? Section 4.1 says human-only participants contributed significantly more ideas, while section 5.1 says there was no significant difference in human idea counts (PDF pp. 6 and 8).
Are participant-level arm SDs, SEs or confidence intervals for the flexibility and fluency contrasts available elsewhere? None are printed, and no supplementary source is identified.
notes: Screened against the complete 10-page PDF and all four contiguous chunks of the markdown on 2026-10-09. Locators use PDF page numbers, with printed proceedings pages added where useful. Outcome inventory: Table 2 reports human-origin and combined-origin idea quantities; Figures 3 and 4 report participant-level category coverage including and excluding accepted AI suggestions; section 4.1 additionally reports within-category fluency and the association between idea number and category coverage; Figure 5/section 4.2 report pooled category coverage/distribution by origin and the rate of introducing new categories. Figure 1 shows the app, Figure 2 the prompt, and Table 1 the category definitions/examples; these add no separate scored outcome. Qualitative perceptions (section 4.3) and request frequency are not output scores and are not coded as outcomes. All seven output measures are retained; none was dropped because of the outcome cap. H1 and H2 flexibility outcomes are marked paper_primary because they are the two explicit hypotheses (PDF p. 4); no preregistration or unique primary-outcome ranking is stated. Although the paper calls flexibility 'diversity', its main measures count categories within each participant's ideas and are coded flexibility, not across_people. The pooled AI-versus-human category analyses do not measure an AI-assistance effect on similarity across different people, and are marked question=none. AI remained available while human-authored ideas were produced, so excluding AI-origin ideas does not make those outcomes after_ai. Table 2's 373 AI suggestions are distinct from the 115 accepted/copied suggestions used in the combined-list flexibility analysis (PDF pp. 5–6); combined logged idea totals are not final accepted-list totals. The setting is coded field_rct because data collection occurred inside university courses (PDF p. 4, section 3.1), not an online panel; the paper does not explicitly label the setting as lab or field. Country is not explicitly stated; the authors' Hamburg affiliation is not substituted for a stated participant country. No public data/code URL is reported. No effect sizes or missing statistics were calculated.
